INTERESTS OF AMICI CURIAE1
 The American Federation of Teachers (“AFT”)
is a union of professionals and AFL-CIO affiliate that
represents more than 1.8 million members in more
than 3,600 local affiliates nationwide. AFT aims to
advance principles of fairness, democracy, health,
high-quality public education, and public services for
students through community engagement, organizing,
and political activism. Combatting gun violence is
essential to advance AFT’s initiative to improve the
public health of our communities and the quality of
public education. AFT has prepared numerous
reports, resources, resolutions, and other materials to
spotlight the important role gun violence reduction
has in creating a proper learning environment for
children in the United States. The legal issues
presented in this case are of interest to AFT because
of the profound importance of upholding restrictions
on semi-automatic weapons for students nationwide.

 The Campaign to Keep Guns Off Campus (“the
Campaign”) looks to support safe educational spaces
nationwide by opposing policies allowing guns on
campus, thereby protecting students from physical
danger. The Campaign has collaborated with
educational institutions at all levels of education, as
well as state legislatures, to work towards their goal.
The allowance of an ordinance barring the sale and

possession of assault weapons clearly falls in line with
the Campaign’s mission to protect campuses from the
threat of gun violence , especially as numerous school
shooters have used the same class of weapon to launch
their attacks.

INTRODUCTION AND SUMMARY OF THE
ARGUMENT

 The Seventh Circuit2 held that Illinois and i ts
localities had a strong likelihood of prevailing against
Second Amendment challenges to their assault -
weapons restrictions, concluding that AR -15s and
similar semiautomatic rifles more closely resemble
military weapons than firearms protected for civilian
use.3 As such, the Seventh Circuit affirmed the
judgment in favor of Cook County, concluding that
petitioners had failed to develop a record sufficient to
depart from the court’s prior decision in Bevis v. City
of Naperville , which rejected a Second Amendment
challenge to another assault-weapons ordinance.

 As more fully elaborated below, the Seventh
Circuit’s decision  is consistent with the Nation’s
historical tradition of firearm regulation and serves
the important interest of protecting students and
educators from gun violence. Cook County’s ordinance
helps preserve schools as environments where
students can learn and educators can educate without

amici’s arguments apply equally to both the Seventh and Second
circuit decisions.
3 Bevis v. City of Naperville, 85 F.4th 1175, 1182 (7th Cir. 2023).

3
the constant threat of armed violence. Amici urge the
Court to affirm the judgments of the court of appeals.

ARGUMENT

I. Cook County’s ordinance fits the Nation’s
tradition of keeping weapons away from
places of education and addresses a
danger that could not have arisen in 1791
or 1868
In 1993, amid growing national concern over
assault-weapon violence following the 1989 shooting
at Cleveland Elementary School in Stockton ,
California, where a gunman killed five children with a
semiautomatic rifle , Cook County enacted an
ordinance prohibiting  the sale and possession of
assault weapons.4 Since then, gunmen with the same
class of rifle have attacked Sandy Hook Elementary,
Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School, Robb
Elementary, and Apalachee High School.5 Each school
was full of children entrusted to the State’s
“temporary custody.” 6 The weapon in every one of
those attacks belonged to the class of assault weapons
Cook County had prohibited years earlier in response
to the Stockton shooting. 7 Petitioners ask this Court
to hold that the Nation’s history forbids that choice by
local legislators and to direct judgment in their favor.

4 Br. in Opp. at 2, 11, Viramontes v. Cook County, No. 25-238 (U.S.
Oct. 29, 2025).
5 Id. at 1-3.
6 Vernonia Sch. Dist. 47J v. Acton, 515 U.S. 646, 654 (1995).
7 Br. in Opp., supra note 4, at 1-3, 11-12.

4
Under this Court’s precedent  for determining
the validity of a firearm re gulation, the question is
whether the ordinance “is consistent with the Nation’s
historical tradition.” 8 That inquiry turns on  whether
the modern law “is consistent with the principles that
underpin our regulatory tradition,” not whether it has
a “historical twin.”9 When the modern law “addresses
a situation that could not have arisen when the Second
or Fourteenth Amendment was adopted, it is too much
to demand such a close match.”10
Cook County’s ordinance satisfies that test. The
danger it addresses—a semi-automatic rifle attack on
schools that children must attend by law —did not
exist in 1791 or 1868. 11 While the ordinance does not
have an exact historical match, it reflects the same
longstanding concern underlying nineteenth-century
laws that barred weapons from places of education :
protecting children from armed violence. The
ordinance carries that tradition forward by addressing
the distinct threat that modern semiautomatic rifles
pose to school safety .12 In Heller, t his Court left
legislatures “a variety of tools” against gun violence,13
and its long respect for local control of public schools
supports Cook County’s choice of a county-wide ban on
the class of rifle at issue.14

8 N.Y. State Rifle & Pistol Ass’n v. Bruen, 597 U.S. 1, 24 (2022).
9 U.S. v. Rahimi, 602 U.S. 680, 692 (2024).
10 Wolford v. Lopez, 609 U.S. 185, 197 (2026).
11 See infra part I.A.
12 See infra part I.B.
13 D.C. v. Heller, 554 U.S. 570, 636 (2008).
14 See infra part I.C.

5
A. A semi-automatic rifle attack on a
school that the State requires children
to attend is a danger that “could not
have arisen” in 1791 or 1868
Semi-automatic r ifle attacks on children
attending school as mandated by the State  are a
modern problem that, under Bruen, does not require a
close historical analogue. In Bruen, this Court
distinguished between longstanding societal problems
and novel regulatory challenges. 15 When a law
“addresses a general societal problem that has
persisted since the 18th century,” the absence of a
“distinctly similar historical regulation” is “relevant
evidence” against its constitutionality.16 However,
“cases implicating unprecedented societal concerns or
dramatic technological changes may require a more
nuanced approach,” because today’s regulatory
challenges “are not always the same as those that
preoccupied the Founders in 1791 or the
Reconstruction generation in 1868.”17 In Wolford, this
Court reaffirmed that  when a  law “addresses a
situation that could not have arisen when the Second
or Fourteenth Amendment was adopted, it is too much
to demand such a close match.” 18 The Court cited
Rahimi, where “distinctively modern” conduct “called
for a more difficult exercise of judgment” in identifying
historical analogues.19

15 Bruen, 597 U.S. at 26-27.
16 Id. at 26.
17 Id. at 27.
18 609 U.S. at 197.
19 Id. at 198.

6
Semi-automatic rifle attacks on schoolchildren
are unique in two ways . The first is the target. When
the Fourteenth Amendment was ratified, “compulsory
school attendance was virtually unknown.” 20 Today,
every State requires children to attend school. 21 More
than 54 million children are enrolled in kindergarten
through twelfth grade, and the average public high
school holds 831 students. 22 The State therefore
requires millions of  children to gather  together in
school buildings each day , where they “have been
committed to the temporary custody of the State as
schoolmaster.”23
That custody carries a special duty. In
Vernonia, th is Court upheld random drug testing of
student athletes as a reasonable search, in part ,
because “the necessity for the State to act is magnified
by the fact that this evil is being visited not just upon
individuals at large, but upon children for whom it has
undertaken a special responsibility of care and
direction.”24 Although Vernonia concerned student

21 See id.  at 490 n.4 (noting that compulsory attendance laws
were “in force in all the states” by 1918).
22 U.S. Census Bureau, School Enrollment: 2024 American
Community Survey 1 -Year Estimates , tbl. S1401,
https://data.census.gov/table/ACSST1Y2024.S1401 (last visited
Oct. 28, 2026); Nat’l Ctr. for Educ. Stat., U.S. Dep’t of Educ.,
Number of Regular Operational Public Schools and Average
Number of Students Enrolled, by School Level and State or
Jurisdiction: School Year 2023 -24,
https://nces.ed.gov/ccd/tables/202324_summary_4.asp (last
visited Oct. 28, 2026).
23 Vernonia Sch. Dist. 47J, 515 U.S. at 654.
24 Id. at 662, 664-65.

7
drug use, the Court rested its reasoning on the State’s
heightened responsibility for children entrusted to its
care.25 Neither the founding nor Reconstruction
generations could have faced a rifle attack on a
building full of children whom the State requires to be
there.
The second difference is the class of arm used in
the attack . The Seventh Circuit, upholding Illinois’s
ban on the same class of rifles, held that at the time of
the Second and Fourteenth Amendments ’
ratifications, “mass killings were a ‘group activity’”
because individuals lacked “the means to inflict mass
casualties on their own .”26 Legislatures therefore
regulated armed groups rather than any particular
weapon. The AR -15, by contrast, was designed to
Army specifications in 1957, and its wounds “are even
more deadly for children.”27
Amici bear the brunt of that duty during every
school day. The teacher is the adult whom the State
has entrusted with the students’ “care and direction”
during the school day.28 Yet, a single individual armed
with a modern semiautomatic rifle can now pose the
threat of mass violence that once required an entire
armed group. 29 Teachers are charged with educating

25 See id. at 662.
26 Barnett v. Raoul, 180 F.4th 1035, 1057 (7th Cir. 2026) (citation
modified).
27 Br. in Opp., supra note 4, at 5-6 (citing R. 81 ¶¶ 75, 298-99).
28 See Vernonia, 515 U.S. at 662.
29 See Darrell A.H. Miller et al., Lethality and the Historical
Principles of Arms Regulation, 54 PEPP. L. REV. (forthcoming)
(manuscript at 29–30, 34–36).

8
children, not preparing them for the possibility of
mass violence. 30 Such preparations may help schools
respond to a threat or an attack, but educators cannot,
on their own, prevent a rifle capable of inflicting mass
casualties from reaching th eir classrooms.
Accordingly, measures like Cook County’s ordinance
serve a critical preventative purpose: confronting that
danger before it materializes and reaches the
schoolhouse door.
The County enacted its ordinance in response to
an attack on an elementary school. 31 Nationwide
compulsory attendance —the sole reason why the
children were in that school —did not exist in 1868,
and the rifle used against them did not exist until
1957.32 The ordinance therefore “addresses a situation
that could not have arisen when the Second or
Fourteenth Amendment was adopted,” and the Court
should not demand “such a close match” to the laws of
that time.33


30 Id. at 38 (observing that school -shooting drills now occur in
95% of schools and are associated with increased depression,
anxiety, and stress).
31 Br. in Opp., supra note 4, at 11-12.
32 Brown, 347 U.S. at 490; Br. in Opp., supra note 4, at 5.
33 Wolford, 609 U.S. at 197; see also Bruen , 597 U.S. at 27
(reserving a “more nuanced approach” for “unprecedented
societal concerns or dramatic technological changes.”)

9
B. The Nation’s tradition of protecting
places of education from armed
violence shares the same purpose as
Cook County’s ordinance
Historical laws addressing a particular problem
are “a strong indicator that contemporary laws
imposing similar restrictions for similar reasons fall
within a permissible category of regulations .”34 The
Nation’s tradition of firearm regulation includes
protecting schools. In Heller, t his Court listed “laws
forbidding the carrying of firearms in sensitive places
such as schools” among the “longstanding” regulations
it left untouched .35 Bruen likewise recognized the
constitutionality of “modern regulations prohibiting
the carry of firearms in new and analogous sensitive
places.”
Legislatures in the n ineteenth-century
specifically protected places of education. In 1870,
Texas barred weapons where people assembled for
“educational, literary or scientific purposes”; Missouri
followed in 1875, and Arizona and the Oklahoma
Territories in 1889 and 1890. 36 The Second Circuit
recognized t hese laws as part of “the tradition of

34 Id.
35 554 U.S. at 626.
36 An Act to Prevent the Carrying of Weapons in Public Assemblies
of the People, § 1, 1875 Mo. Laws 50, 50 -51; see also Antonyuk v.
James, 120 F.4th 941, 1020 (2d Cir. 2024) (quoting 1870 Tex.
Gen. Laws 63, ch. 46; 1883 Mo. Sess. Laws 76; 1889 Ariz. Sess.
Laws 17; 1890 Okla. Terr. Stats., art. 47, § 7).

10
prohibiting firearms in schools” and noted their reason
was “the protection of vulnerable populations.”37
Cook County enacted its ordinance for the same
reason, taking action  in the wake of the Cleveland
Park Elementary assault weapon massacre where a
gunman with a semiautomatic rifle killed five children
in California in 1993.38 In adopting its ordinance, the
Cook County Board cited an estimate  that “1 in 20
high school students had carried a gun in the prior
month.”39
Similarly, f our months after the Sandy Hook
shooting, Connecticut enacted “An Act Concerning
Gun Violence Prevention and Children’s Safety,”40 the
legislation underlying  the Second Circuit’s decision.
Texas in 1870, Cook County in 1993, and Connecticut
in 2013  each sought to protect children from  deadly
weapons, reflecting a shared regulatory purpose
relevant to the “strong indicator” this Court described
in Rahimi.41 The tradition reache s the educator as
well as the student ; i n 1878, Mississippi made it a
misdemeanor for “any teacher, instructor, or professor

37 Antonyuk, 120 F.4th at 1011.
38 Br. in Opp., supra note 4, at 11.
39 Wilson v. Cook County , 407 Ill. App. 3d 759, 761 (2011)
(describing the findings in Cook County Ordinance No. 93 -O-
37(1993)), aff’d in part, rev’d in part, 2012 IL 112026, 968 N.E.2d
641.
40 2013 Conn. Pub. Acts 13 -3; see Nat’l Ass’n for Gun Rights v.
Lamont, 153 F.4th 213, 222 (2d Cir. 2025), cert. granted sub nom.
Grant v. Higgins, No. 25-566 (U.S. June 30, 2026).
41 602 U.S. at 692.

11
who shall, knowingly, suffer or permit any such
weapon to be carried by any student or pupil.”42
Although the means of enforcement differs, the
difference reasonably follows from consideration of the
danger’s modern and previously unencountered
nature. A place-based rule already exists. Federal law
makes it a crime “knowingly to possess a firearm” in a
“school zone.” 43 The nineteenth -century laws barred
carrying a weapon into places of education, while Cook
County’s ordinance bars possessing one class of
weapon anywhere in the County —both are place -
based laws which account for a specific danger. Sandy
Hook, Marjory Stoneman Douglas, Robb Elementary,
and Apalachee were all school zones on the day a
gunman carried a semiautomatic rifle inside. The
County simply responded to th e magnitude of the
danger when enacting its ordinance—it altered the
place of such restriction to protect schoolchildren from
attacks involving assault rifles , accounting for
advances in firearms technology that had reduced the
effectiveness of existing protections.
By the time a school -zone rule applies, it is too
late—the gunman is  already inside. At Robb
Elementary, while the children “were dying,” officers
outside “focused on calls for additional SWAT
equipment.”44 Further, the rifle in school shootings
usually comes from the home. In the Secret Service’s

42 An Act to Prevent the Carrying of Concealed Weapons, and for
Other Purposes, ch. 46, § 4, 1878 Miss. Laws 175, 176.
43 18 U.S.C. § 922(q)(2)(A) (2026).
44 U.S. Dep’t of Just., Critical Incident Review: Active Shooter at
Robb Elementary School xvii (2024).

12
study of school attacks from 2008 through 2017, three
quarters of the attackers who used a firearm took it
from the home of a parent or another close relative. 45
By targeting possession in the community,  Cook
County addressed the danger at an earlier poin t,
cutting the issue at the root rather than the stem.
The difference in means is acceptable under
this Court’s jurisprudence.  In Rahimi, this Court
upheld a modern law whose means differed in kind
from the founding-era laws that justified it: 18 U.S.C.
§ 922(g)(8)  prohibits firearm possession by those
under a domestic -violence restraining order, a court
order that did not exist at the founding.  The
government defended the law with two kinds of
founding-era laws: surety laws requiring a person who
threatened another to post bond, and “going armed”
laws imprisoning those who terrified the public with
weapons.46 Those laws imposed bonds and prison
terms, not a ban on possession. The Court nonetheless
found § 922(g)(8) “relevantly similar” to them in “both
why and how,” because it “restricts gun use to mitigate
demonstrated threats of physical violence, just as th e
surety and going armed laws do,” and because “if
imprisonment was permissible to respond to the use of
guns to threaten the physical safety of others, then the
lesser restriction of temporary disarmament that

45 U.S. Secret Serv., Nat’l Threat Assessment Ctr., Protecting
America’s Schools: A U.S. Secret Service Analysis of Targeted
School Violence  22 (2019),
https://www.secretservice.gov/sites/default/files/2020-
04/Protecting_Americas_Schools.pdf.
46 Rahimi, 602 U.S. at 695-99.

13
Section 922(g)(8) imposes is also permissible.” 47 The
Court thus held upheld the arms ban.48
The same reasoning applies here. The 18 00s
laws and Cook County’s ordinance share a reason :
keeping deadly weapons away from people gathered to
learn. They differ in means : a ban on carrying at the
place versus a ban on possessing one class of arms
across the County. The ordinance reaches a wider area
than a school-zone rule but a narrower set of weapons,
since it allows every handgun, shotgun, and rifle
without the listed f eatures. In Rahimi, the modern
means was different in kind from the historical means,
and the Court still found the laws “relevantly
similar.”49 When the reason is shared and the modern
means fits the modern danger, such as in this case and
Rahimi, the “how” and “why” are “close enough.”50
C. The tradition of local control over
public schools supports Cook County’s
choice among the “variety of tools” this
Court recognized in Heller
This Court acknowledged in Heller “the
problem of handgun violence in this country” and
noted the Constitution leaves “a variety of tools for
combating that problem.” 51 In Heller, this Court
named schools first among the places where the

47 Id. at 698-99.
48 Id. at 702.
49 Id. at 698.
50 Wolford, 609 U.S. at 197.
51 554 U.S. at 636.

14
Second Amendment right yields52 and left legislatures
“a variety of tools” against gun violence. 53 Cook
County’s ordinance chose one . It answers a danger
that did not exist when either the Second or the
Fourteenth Amendment was adopted, and it serves
the same purpose as the nineteenth-century laws that
kept weapons away from places of education.54
Under Bruen, the only question is whether the
law fits the tradition. 55 In asking whether a
community’s “how” is “close enough,” the Court should
weigh who made the choice and why. “No single
tradition in public education is more deeply rooted
than local control over the operation of schools; local
autonomy has long been thought essential both to the
maintenance of community concern and support for
public schools and to quality of the educational
process.”56 Education is also an area “in which this
Court’s lack of specialized knowledge and experience
counsels against premature interference with the
informed judgments made at the state and local
levels.”57
Cook County made that choice twice : once  in
1993 after the California attack and the second time

popularity overlooks the distinctive
dangers these weapons pose to schools

the AR -15 rests on one number. They  describe it  as

Essentially, petitioners ask this Court to treat
the widespread ownership of AR -15-style rifles as
dispositive of their constitutional protection. But a
national count of rifle owners cannot resolve whether
a regulation is consistent with the Nation’s historical
tradition of firearm regulation. As this Court
explained in Bruen and Rahimi, that inquiry requires
consideration of the reasons underlying historical
restrictions and the burdens they imposed, not merely
the prevalence of the regulated conduct. Part I  above
explained why the challenged  legislation are
consistent with the historical tradition of protecting
schools and other sensitive places. This Part now
addresses the distinctively modern danger that gives
that tradition continuing significance.
A. Semiautomatic rifles pose  a
disproportionate danger in school
shootings

Petitioners measure the AR-15’s danger
primarily through national homicide statistics . They
observe that rifles of every kind are used in fewer
homicides annually than handguns and conclude that
the AR -15 rifle is rarely used in crime .63 However,

these weapons pose in school shootings, where the

The FBI recorded thirty active-shooter
situations in kindergarten through twelfth grade
school environments between September 2004 and
December 2025 that left three or more people killed or
wounded.64 Eleven of those incidents (about a third )
involved a semi-automatic rifle meeting the definition
of “assault weapon” in the Protect Illinois
Communities Act.65 Those eleven incidents account for
more than half of all casualties and nearly two -thirds
of all deaths across the thirty  shootings.66 Incidents
involving these rifles averaged roughly twice as many
casualties as the others and nearly three times as
many deaths ; half  of the people shot in them were
killed, compared with about a third in the remaining
incidents.67

These figures reveal a  disparity that national
homicide statistics conceal. Active-shooter incidents
involving semi -automatic rifles usually means  more
people are wounded and killed  and lead to
substantially greater casualties when used in school

The consequences of these attacks are pointedly
more significant in the school setting. Unlike most
adults who may choose whether to enter particular
public spaces, children are required by law to attend
school, and the educators who staff those buildings are

AR-15 as beyond the reach of regulation because many
people own one would leave the communities
responsible for those schools unable to address the
weapon behind the worst attacks on them . Where a
locality has identified a specific, documented harm
associated with a weapon, widespread ownership
alone should not foreclose its ability to adopt
legislation consistent with its duty to uphold public
safety.

becomes immune from regulation once it sells widely
enough. This Court has never so held . Under

B. The threat of school shootings imposes
lasting psychological, educational, and
institutional burdens on students and
educators

The harm associated with school shootings
extends far beyond the immediate victims. The
possibility of an attack has altered the daily
experience of students and educators, requiring
schools to devote substantial attention and resources
to preparing for violence rather than educating
children.
For educators, the threat is neither abstract nor
confined to communities that have experienced a
shooting. In 2023, Pew Research Center surveyed over
2,500 K -12 teachers  and found that 23  percent of
teachers experienced a gun -related lockdown at their

20
school in the prior school year. 71 Among high school
teachers, that number was as high as one in three (34
percent), and 12 percent reported that there was more
than one lockdown due to the possession or suspicion
of a gun on school grounds during the year. 72 These
frequent threats cause real, widespread fear among
teachers; 59 percent of teachers are at least somewhat
worried about a shooting at their school, with 18
percent of teachers being extremely or very worried.73

In 2024, another survey of over 1,000 teachers
found that their fear of being attacked at school grew
over time, increasing from 17 percent in 2022 to 24
percent in 2023.74 While that statistic includes fear of
harm from any source, other research indicates that
school shootings are a likely cause. One study found
that a majority (52 percent) of teachers who feared for
their safety at school cited fear of an active shooter as
a reason, making it the second-most common concern,
only 1  percent behind student misbehavior (53
percent).75

C. Active shooter drills and security
measures harm students’  mental
health and education

The frequency of school shootings in the United
States necessitates that schools prepare students and
staff for active shooter scenarios. Active-shooter drills
and lockdown procedures have become routine
features of U.S. education. Data from the Department
of Education indicates that 96.2  percent of public
schools have a written plan for active shooter
scenarios, and nearly 96 percent have drilled students
on lockdowns due to immediate threats of violence. 78
While the implementation of active shooter drills may
be well -intentioned, more frequent drills cause
educators to feel less safe and more likely to consider
quitting teaching.79

Although intended to protect students and
educators, these measures can also reinforce the fear
that violence may erupt in spaces dedicated to
learning. A study of around fifty-four million social
media posts from K-12 school communities before and
after school shooter drills showed a 42.1  percent
increase in anxiety and 38.7  percent increase in

As such, the harm caused by gun violence in
schools is compounded by the effects of the measures
taken to prepare for and prevent it.  The need to
prepare for the possibility of school shootings imposes
psychological and institutional burdens, forcing
schools to divert resources from education and
subjecting students and educators to the stress and
anxiety of repeated emergency preparations.  For the
Nation’s schools, even when no shots are fired, the
mere threat of school gun violence exacts a heavy toll.

CONCLUSION

 For the foregoing reasons, the judgments of the
courts of appeals should be affirmed.
